sections.body_md:
A Taylor model replaces a function near a chosen point by a polynomial that matches its derivatives there. The first-order model matches the value and the gradient. Its graph is the tangent affine approximation. The second-order model also matches the Hessian, so the slice in every direction matches curvature as well as slope.

Both models are functions of the new point. They are built entirely from information at the expansion point. The factor one half in front of the Hessian term is what makes a further differentiation return the Hessian rather than twice the Hessian.

The errors shrink at different rates. After the value and the gradient have been matched, the error of the linear model is little-o of the step length. After the Hessian has been matched too, and the second derivatives are continuous, the error of the quadratic model is little-o of the squared step length. Those statements are about small steps. At one particular step the quadratic model can still miss by more than the linear model.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(h = y - x\),
\[
T_1(y) = f(x) + \nabla f(x)^{T} h, \qquad T_2(y) = T_1(y) + \tfrac12 h^{T} H_f(x)\, h.
\]
If \(f\) is differentiable, \(f(y) - T_1(y) = o(\lVert h \rVert)\). If the second partials are continuous, \(f(y) - T_2(y) = o(\lVert h \rVert^2)\). On a quadratic polynomial, \(T_2\) is exact.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
On the cubic slice at x = 2, let \(f(x, y) = y^3 + x\), expanded at \((2, 3)\) with step \((0, -1)\). The value is \(27 + 2 = 29\). The gradient is \((1, 3 y^2) = (1, 27)\), so the linear term is \(-27\). The only nonzero second partial is \(\partial^2 f / \partial y^2 = 6y = 18\), and the quadratic term is \(\tfrac12 \cdot 18 \cdot 1 = 9\). The second-order model is
\[
29 - 27 + 9 = 11.
\]
The function at the new point \((2, 2)\) is \(8 + 2 = 10\). The model used derivatives only at the expansion point. A cubic is allowed to miss the model at a step of this length.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Dropping the one half doubles the quadratic term and makes the Hessian of the model twice the Hessian of \(f\). Evaluating the gradient or the Hessian at the new point is a different formula, closer to an exact expansion with an intermediate point. The linear model is not the gradient; the gradient is only the coefficient of the step. Little-o statements do not rank the two models at one fixed step.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The exact second-order expansion keeps the same shape and moves the Hessian to an intermediate point, which is how a bound is proved. Newton's method minimizes the quadratic model and solves \(H d = -\nabla f\). A backtracking line search uses only the linear model, and it accepts a step whose true decrease covers a fraction of the predicted linear decrease.
